etymology: Hebrew 'Uzziyyah, “the LORD is my strength,” from 'oz (strength) and Yah (the covenant name); also called Azariah in the books of Kings.
biblical_def: Uzziah was the tenth king of Judah, son of Amaziah, who reigned fifty-two years and did that which was right in the sight of the LORD so long as he sought God in the days of Zechariah his counsellor. Under the blessing of God he prospered greatly: he subdued the Philistines and the Arabians, built towers in Jerusalem and the wilderness, digged many wells, loved husbandry, and fashioned engines of war upon the walls. His name spread far abroad, for he was marvellously helped till he was strong. But the Chronicler will not flatter him. When he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction, and he transgressed against the LORD his God by going into the temple to burn incense upon the altar of incense—the office reserved for the sons of Aaron alone. Azariah the priest and fourscore valiant priests withstood him, and while he raged against them the leprosy rose up in his forehead before the very altar. He was a leper unto the day of his death, cut off from the house of the LORD, dwelling in a several house while Jotham his son judged the people. It was in the year that king Uzziah died that Isaiah saw the LORD high and lifted up, the throne of heaven undimmed though an earthly throne lay empty. His reign is the standing warning of the dictionary's confessional standard: prosperity is the soul's most dangerous hour, and presumption upon the holy things of God is no light sin but a leprous one.
webster_summary: The long-reigning king of Judah who prospered while he sought the LORD but was struck with leprosy for usurping the priestly office; his death-year framed Isaiah's vision of the throne of God.
webster_full: UZZIAH, proper noun. [Hebrew, the LORD is my strength.] The tenth king of Judah, son of Amaziah, also named Azariah; reigned fifty and two years.
He sought God in the days of Zechariah and was prospered in war, building, and husbandry, so that his name spread far abroad.
Being strong, his heart was lifted up, and he intruded into the temple to burn incense, an office belonging to the priests alone.
For this presumption the leprosy smote him in the forehead, and he dwelt a leper in a several house until his death.
In the year of his death the prophet Isaiah beheld the LORD upon a throne, high and lifted up (Isaiah 6:1).
scriptures: And he sought God in the days of Zechariah, who had understanding in the visions of God: and as long as he sought the LORD, God made him to prosper.
But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction: for he transgressed against the LORD his God, and went into the temple of the LORD to burn incense upon the altar of incense.

And Uzziah the king was a leper unto the day of his death, and dwelt in a several house, being a leper; for he was cut off from the house of the LORD: and Jotham his son was over the king's house, judging the people of the land.
Isa 6:1
In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is rather the flattening of the Chronicler's moral verdict into a tale of mere political success.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that prosperity is a trial, not a reward to be presumed upon. The modern reader, schooled to measure a reign by its building projects and military gains, would write Uzziah down as one of Judah's great success stories and pass over the altar of incense in a footnote. The Chronicler will not. The same hand that grew strong reached into the sanctuary, and the God who had helped him struck him before the altar he profaned. Strength tempted him; it tempts still.

Where modern Ancient-Near-Eastern history would subordinate the theological judgment to the metrics of statecraft, the dictionary holds the Chronicler's verdict as its own: the reign was right in the eyes of the LORD until the heart was lifted up, and then it was leprous. The closed sanctuary and the empty throne of Isaiah 6 belong together; the year Uzziah died, the prophet saw the throne that no leprosy can empty and no presumption can climb.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew 'oz (strength) and Yah (the covenant name), “the LORD is my strength”; the kingly name Azariah, “the LORD has helped,” is its companion.
roots_lines: 'Uzziyyah, Hebrew, “the LORD is my strength,” from 'oz, strength.
Yah, the shortened form of the covenant name YHWH, appended to many Judahite royal names.
Azaryah (Azariah), “the LORD has helped,” the alternate name in the books of Kings.
The verb of 2 Chronicles 26:15, “he was marvellously helped, till he was strong,” turns the helping of God into the occasion of pride.
The leprosy (Hebrew tsara'ath) is the same defiling plague that excluded a man from the camp and the sanctuary.
usage: He warned the young deacon that the years of growing strength are the years of greatest peril, and named Uzziah at the altar.
The sermon paired the empty throne of Judah with the filled throne of Isaiah 6, that the people might fear God and not the changes of state.
She read the reign of Uzziah and saw that the leprosy began in the heart long before it broke out in the forehead.

etymology: Hebrew Golyath, of uncertain Philistine origin, possibly “exile” or “splendour”; the giant of Gath who defied the armies of the living God.
biblical_def: Goliath was the Philistine champion of Gath, a giant six cubits and a span in height, clad in a coat of mail weighing five thousand shekels of brass, whose spear's staff was like a weaver's beam. For forty days, morning and evening, he stood in the valley of Elah and defied the armies of Israel, challenging any man to single combat, and Saul and all Israel were dismayed and greatly afraid. The defiance was not merely martial but blasphemous: he defied the armies of the living God, reproaching the LORD by reproaching His people. David, a youth come from the sheepfolds with bread and cheese for his brethren, heard the reproach and burned, not for his own honour but for the name of the LORD of hosts. He refused Saul's armour and went down with sling and five smooth stones, declaring that the battle is the LORD'S, who saveth not with sword and spear. One stone sank into the giant's forehead, and David cut off his head with the Philistine's own sword. The combat is no fable of the underdog but a covenant pattern: the seed of the woman bruising the head of the serpent's champion, the weak thing of the world confounding the mighty, that all the earth may know there is a God in Israel. Goliath stands forever as the type of every proud power that defies the living God and is brought down by the despised instrument of His choosing.
webster_summary: The Philistine giant of Gath who defied the armies of the living God and was slain by David with a sling and a stone; the standing type of proud power humbled by the weak thing God chooses.
webster_full: GOLIATH, proper noun. The champion of the Philistines, of Gath, six cubits and a span in height, who defied the armies of Israel in the valley of Elah.
He challenged any Israelite to single combat for forty days, and his defiance was a reproach against the living God.
David the shepherd, refusing Saul's armour, went against him with a sling and five smooth stones in the name of the LORD of hosts.
A single stone smote him in the forehead, and David slew him and cut off his head with the giant's own sword.
Figuratively, any towering and blasphemous power that the LORD brings low by an instrument the world counts contemptible.
scriptures: And there went out a champion out of the camp of the Philistines, named Goliath, of Gath, whose height was six cubits and a span.

Then said David to the Philistine, Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied.

This day will the LORD deliver thee into mine hand; and I will smite thee, and take thine head from thee; and I will give the carcases of the host of the Philistines this day unto the fowls of the air, and to the wild beasts of the earth; that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel.
And all this assembly shall know that the LORD saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle is the LORD'S, and he will give you into our hands.
corruption_summary: The popular “David and Goliath” trope empties the account of God and reduces it to a parable of plucky human courage overcoming long odds.
corruption_paragraphs: The phrase “a David-and-Goliath story” has been wholly secularized into a tale of the underdog whose grit and ingenuity topple the favourite. This is a corruption by omission. David himself forbids the reading: the battle is the LORD'S, and the victory is given that all the earth may know there is a God in Israel. To make the account a lesson in self-belief is to put David in the place of God and to silence the very confession the text was written to provoke.

Read in the line of Scripture, the combat is covenantal and typological. The reproach was against the living God; the deliverer was the LORD's anointed, despised by his brethren and refused the world's armour; the weapon was the weak thing that confounds the mighty (1 Corinthians 1:27). Here is the protoevangelium pattern—the appointed seed crushing the head of the enemy—and the gospel pattern of the cross, where God saved not with sword and spear but with what the world called weakness.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew Golyath, a Philistine name of disputed sense; the dictionary's interest is in the theology of the combat, not the philology of a heathen name.
roots_lines: Golyath, Hebrew transcription of a Philistine name, perhaps from a root meaning to lay bare or to go into exile.
Gath, one of the five Philistine cities, later the home of other giants of the sons of Anak.
The “cubit and a span” measure marks his stature as monstrous against the ordinary height of a man.
Cherpah, Hebrew, reproach, the word for the defiance Goliath heaped upon the armies of God.
The five smooth stones from the brook are the despised instrument that the LORD chose to confound the mighty.
usage: The pastor told the children that the stone flew true because the battle was the LORD'S, not because David was brave.
He warned against preaching Goliath as a motivational tale, for David preached God and not himself.
When the small congregation faced the towering threat, the elder read 1 Samuel 17 and reminded them the LORD saveth not with sword and spear.

etymology: Hebrew Chaza'el, “God has seen,” from chazah (to see) and El (God); the Syrian who murdered his master to seize the throne of Damascus.
biblical_def: Hazael was a servant of Ben-hadad king of Syria whom the LORD marked out, through Elijah and afterward Elisha, to be the rod of His chastisement upon faithless Israel. When the Lord at Horeb commissioned Elijah, He named Hazael to be anointed king over Syria, an instrument of judgment alongside Jehu and Elisha. The dreadful scene of his rise is recorded when sick Ben-hadad sent him to inquire of Elisha whether he should recover. The prophet fixed his countenance upon Hazael until he was ashamed, and the man of God wept, for he foresaw the evil Hazael would do to the children of Israel: their strong holds set on fire, their young men slain, their children dashed, their women with child ripped up. Hazael, feigning humility, protested, “Is thy servant a dog, that he should do this great thing?” yet the next day he smothered his master with a wet cloth and reigned in his stead. Thereafter the LORD began to cut Israel short, and Hazael oppressed them all the days of Jehoahaz. Hazael is the dictionary's standing case that God ordains even the wicked as the instruments of His righteous judgment without being the author of their sin—the murderer is fully guilty, and yet the sword he wields is the sword the LORD appointed against a covenant people who would not repent.
webster_summary: The Syrian servant who murdered Ben-hadad and seized the throne of Damascus, foreseen by Elisha as the LORD's rod of judgment upon apostate Israel; a study in God's sovereign use of a guilty instrument.
webster_full: HAZAEL, proper noun. [Hebrew, God has seen.] A servant of Ben-hadad king of Syria, afterward king of Damascus.
Elijah was charged at Horeb to anoint him king over Syria, one of three instruments of judgment upon Israel.
Sent to Elisha concerning his master's sickness, he heard the prophet foretell the evil he would work upon Israel, and Elisha wept.
He murdered Ben-hadad with a wet cloth and reigned in his stead, then oppressed Israel all his days.
An example of a wicked man whom God ordains as the rod of His chastisement, guilty in his sin yet serving the divine purpose.
scriptures: And the LORD said unto him, Go, return on thy way to the wilderness of Damascus: and when thou comest, anoint Hazael to be king over Syria.

And Hazael said, Why weepeth my lord? And he answered, Because I know the evil that thou wilt do unto the children of Israel: their strong holds wilt thou set on fire, and their young men wilt thou slay with the sword, and wilt dash their children, and rip up their women with child.
And Hazael said, But what, is thy servant a dog, that he should do this great thing? And Elisha answered, The LORD hath shewed me that thou shalt be king over Syria.
In those days the LORD began to cut Israel short: and Hazael smote them in all the coasts of Israel.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the squeamish refusal to confess that God sovereignly ordains wicked instruments of judgment while holding them wholly guilty.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the hard, comforting doctrine of providence over the wicked. The modern mind recoils from a God who names a murderer beforehand and weeps not over the LORD's decree but over the sin of the man. Yet Scripture holds both without flinching: the LORD appointed Hazael as His rod (1 Kings 19:15), and Hazael is fully guilty of the blood he shed. God is not the author of sin; He ordains its bounds and bends even the cruelty of nations to the chastening of His people.

Hazael also exposes the deceit of the human heart. “Is thy servant a dog, that he should do this great thing?” he asked, certain he could never sink so low—and committed the murder within a day. The man who cannot imagine himself capable of a sin is the man nearest to it. The dictionary names this as the total depravity the confession teaches: not that every man is as wicked as he could be, but that no chamber of the heart is exempt, and self-trust is the surest road to the crime one swore one would never commit.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew chazah (to see, to behold in vision) and El (God), “God has seen”—a name of irony over a man whose deeds God saw and judged.
roots_lines: Chaza'el, Hebrew, “God has seen,” from chazah, to see or behold.
El, the general Semitic name for God, here joined to the verb of seeing.
Ben-hadad, “son of Hadad,” the dynastic name of the Syrian kings he served and slew.
The “rod” imagery of Isaiah 10:5 illumines Hazael's office: the heathen power as the staff of God's indignation.
The wet cloth (Hebrew makber, a coverlet) is the homely instrument of the regicide recorded in 2 Kings 8:15.
usage: The elder cited Hazael to show that God may ordain a wicked nation as His rod without ever being the author of its cruelty.
“Is thy servant a dog?” the preacher quoted, then warned that the heart most sure it cannot fall is the heart nearest the fall.
She trembled to read that Elisha wept, not over God's decree, but over the evil a man would freely choose.

pos: proper noun (the last king of Syria)
etymology: Hebrew Retsin, of uncertain meaning, perhaps “firm” or “prince”; the last king of Damascus, confederate with Pekah against Judah.
biblical_def: Rezin was the last king of Syria at Damascus, who joined himself with Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of the northern tribes, in the Syro-Ephraimite war against Ahaz of Judah. The two kings came up to Jerusalem to war, purposing to depose the house of David and set a puppet, the son of Tabeal, upon the throne. The heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people were moved as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind. Into this terror the LORD sent Isaiah with his son Shear-jashub to meet Ahaz, bidding him take heed and be quiet, and fear not for the two tails of these smoking firebrands, the fierce anger of Rezin and Remaliah's son. For though they had taken evil counsel, it should not stand nor come to pass. It was in this crisis that the LORD gave the sign of Immanuel: a virgin should conceive and bear a son, and before the child should know to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land of the two kings Ahaz abhorred should be forsaken. So it came: within a few years Tiglath-pileser of Assyria took Damascus, carried its people captive, and slew Rezin. The dictionary marks Rezin as a smoking firebrand—a threat fearsome in the eyes of unbelief, a spent ember in the counsel of God, whose end is fixed by the Word that gave the sign of Immanuel.
webster_summary: The last king of Damascus, confederate with Pekah against Judah in the Syro-Ephraimite war; the “smoking firebrand” whose threat occasioned the prophecy of Immanuel and whose kingdom Assyria soon destroyed.
webster_full: REZIN, proper noun. The last king of Syria, reigning at Damascus in the days of Ahaz of Judah.
He allied with Pekah king of Israel to make war on Jerusalem and to set the son of Tabeal upon David's throne.
His threat terrified Ahaz, but Isaiah called him and his ally two smoking firebrands whose counsel would not stand.
In this crisis the LORD gave the sign of Immanuel (Isaiah 7:14), the virgin's son.
Assyria under Tiglath-pileser took Damascus and slew Rezin, fulfilling the prophet's word.
scriptures: Then Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel came up to Jerusalem to war: and they besieged Ahaz, but could not overcome him.
Isa 7:4
And say unto him, Take heed, and be quiet; fear not, neither be fainthearted for the two tails of these smoking firebrands, for the fierce anger of Rezin with Syria, and of the son of Remaliah.
Isa 7:14
Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
Isa 8:6
Forasmuch as this people refuseth the waters of Shiloah that go softly, and rejoice in Rezin and Remaliah's son.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the temptation is to read the Immanuel sign as exhausted in Ahaz's day, severing it from the virgin birth of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The historical-critical habit, however, would confine Isaiah 7:14 wholly to a young woman of Ahaz's court and deny it any reach to the Christ. The dictionary rejects that confinement on the authority of Matthew 1:23, which declares the prophecy fulfilled in the virgin birth of the Lord Jesus. The near sign concerning Rezin's firebrand and the far sign of Immanuel are not rivals; the deliverance of the house of David from two spent embers is the pledge and pattern of the greater deliverance the virgin's Son would bring.

Rezin himself is the principle to recover: the fearful threat that unbelief magnifies and faith measures by the Word of God. Ahaz saw two kings and trembled like a forest in the wind; Isaiah saw two stubs of smoking sticks already burning out. The believer is called to take heed, be quiet, and fear not, for the counsel of the heathen, however terrible, shall not stand against the purpose of the LORD.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew Retsin, a Syrian royal name of disputed sense; the prophetic figure of the “smoking firebrand” (Hebrew 'ud) carries the entry's weight.
roots_lines: Retsin, Hebrew, the name of the Damascene king, of uncertain etymology.
'Ud, Hebrew, a firebrand or charred stick snatched from the fire, the image of Isaiah 7:4.
The “waters of Shiloah that go softly” symbolize the quiet rule of the house of David, refused by the people.
Immanu'el, “God with us,” the name of the promised sign-child of Isaiah 7:14.
Tiglath-pileser, the Assyrian conqueror whose campaign ended Rezin and the kingdom of Damascus.
usage: The teacher showed how the threat of Rezin became the occasion of the greatest of the Immanuel prophecies.
“Two smoking firebrands,” the pastor said, “is how God measures the powers that make His people tremble.”
She took comfort that the counsel against the house of David did not stand, for the Lord had spoken Immanuel.

etymology: From Zarephath (Hebrew Tsarephath, “smelting place”), a town of Zidon; the Greek of Luke renders it Sarepta. The widow whom God commanded to sustain Elijah in the famine.
biblical_def: The widow of Zarephath was a Gentile woman of Zidon whom the LORD appointed to sustain Elijah during the three-year famine of Ahab's reign. When the brook Cherith dried up, God sent His prophet not to a daughter of Israel but to a heathen city, that mercy might be shown beyond the covenant nation. Elijah found her at the gate gathering two sticks, with but a handful of meal in a barrel and a little oil in a cruse, preparing a last meal for herself and her son that they might eat it and die. The prophet bade her fear not, and make him a little cake first, upon the word of the LORD that the barrel of meal should not waste nor the cruse of oil fail until rain returned to the earth. She believed and obeyed, putting the man of God's word before her own famished child, and the meal and oil failed not many days. When afterward her son fell sick and died, Elijah stretched himself upon the child and cried unto the LORD, and the soul of the child came into him again—the first raising of the dead recorded in Scripture. Our Lord Himself appealed to her in the synagogue at Nazareth, that Elias was sent to none of the widows of Israel save unto a woman of Sidon, to rebuke the unbelief of His own and to declare that the mercy of God overleaps the bounds of natural Israel. She is the dictionary's early type of Gentile inclusion: a heathen widow who lived by faith in the bare word of God and saw the dead raised.
webster_summary: The Gentile widow of Sidon who fed Elijah from her failing barrel of meal at the word of the LORD, saw the meal and oil unfailing, and received her dead son raised; a type of Gentile inclusion cited by Christ at Nazareth.
webster_full: WIDOW OF ZAREPHATH, noun phrase. A Gentile widow of Zarephath in Sidon, divinely appointed to sustain the prophet Elijah in the famine.
She had but a handful of meal and a little oil, and was preparing a last meal for herself and her son.
At Elijah's word she fed the prophet first, and the meal and oil failed not until the rain returned.
Her son died and was raised when Elijah stretched himself upon him and cried unto the LORD.
Christ named her at Nazareth (Luke 4:26) as a sign that God's mercy reaches beyond natural Israel to the Gentiles.
scriptures: Arise, get thee to Zarephath, which belongeth to Zidon, and dwell there: behold, I have commanded a widow woman there to sustain thee.

And she said, As the LORD thy God liveth, I have not a cake, but an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse: and, behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and dress it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die.
And the barrel of meal wasted not, neither did the cruse of oil fail, according to the word of the LORD, which he spake by Elijah.
But unto none of them was Elias sent, save unto Sarepta, a city of Sidon, unto a woman that was a widow.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is to make her merely a tale of charity or of feminine resilience, missing the faith in the bare word of God and the Gentile mercy her story announces.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is justifying faith resting on nothing but the promise of God. The widow had a single meal between her household and starvation, yet at Elijah's word she gave the prophet's portion first. This is not reckless generosity but the obedience of faith: she staked her last bread on the word of the LORD that the barrel should not waste, and the LORD honoured His word. To read her as a lesson in human kindness or in womanly grit is to lose the gospel in her story.

Her account also rebukes the parochialism that would confine the mercy of God to the natural seed. Our Lord pressed this very point in the synagogue at Nazareth and was nearly thrown from a cliff for it: that Elias passed over many widows in Israel and was sent to a Gentile of Sidon. So God prepared, centuries before, a witness that the gospel would go to the nations, and that a heathen widow living by faith would shame the unbelief of the covenant people. She belongs with Rahab and Ruth among the foretokens of Gentile inclusion.
roots_summary: From Zarephath (Hebrew Tsarephath, “a place of smelting or refining”), a town of Zidon; the famine sets the refining of her faith over the refining furnace her town was named for.
roots_lines: Tsarephath, Hebrew, “smelting place” or “refinery,” a town of the Sidonian coast.
Sarepta, the Greek form of the name as quoted by Luke 4:26.
Almanah, Hebrew, a widow, one of the classes of the helpless God commands His people to defend.
The “barrel” (Hebrew kad) and “cruse” (tsappachath) are the humble vessels through which God multiplied bread.
Elijah's raising of her son is the first resurrection from the dead recorded in the canon.
usage: The pastor preached the widow of Zarephath to teach that faith gives God the first portion and trusts His bare word for the rest.
He reminded the congregation that Christ Himself named her to prove that the mercy of God reaches the Gentiles.
She found in the unfailing barrel of meal a parable of the daily bread that never fails the household of faith.

etymology: Hebrew 'Achiyyah, “brother of the LORD” or “the LORD is my brother,” with ha-Shiloni, the man of Shiloh, the old sanctuary town of Ephraim.
biblical_def: Ahijah the Shilonite was a prophet of the LORD from Shiloh, where the tabernacle had stood in the days of Eli, who spoke the word of God at the breaking of the united kingdom and again at the breaking of the house that rent it. Meeting Jeroboam in the way, he clad himself with a new garment and rent it into twelve pieces, bidding the servant of Solomon take ten, for thus saith the LORD: He would rend the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon—for the idolatry his strange wives had drawn him into—and give ten tribes to Jeroboam, leaving one tribe to David's house for the LORD's servant David's sake and for Jerusalem's sake. Yet the same prophet who promised Jeroboam a sure house if he would walk in God's ways pronounced that house's doom when Jeroboam set up his calves at Bethel and Dan. When Jeroboam's child sickened, he sent his wife in disguise to old and blind Ahijah; but the LORD warned the prophet, and he greeted her at the door with heavy tidings: the child should die, and the dynasty be swept away as a man sweepeth dung. Ahijah is the dictionary's witness that prophecy is no respecter of the powers it once announced: the same mouth that anointed a king for God's purpose condemned him for his apostasy, for the word of the LORD stands above every throne it raises and casts down.
webster_summary: The prophet of Shiloh who foretold the division of the kingdom by rending a new garment into twelve pieces for Jeroboam, and afterward pronounced the doom of Jeroboam's house for its idolatry; a witness that the prophetic word judges even the kings it raises.
webster_full: AHIJAH THE SHILONITE, proper noun. A prophet of the LORD from Shiloh in the reigns of Solomon and Jeroboam.
He met Jeroboam and rent a new garment into twelve pieces, giving him ten as a sign of the ten tribes.
He declared the kingdom rent from Solomon for idolatry, one tribe left to David's house for the LORD's sake.
When Jeroboam fell into the sin of the calves, Ahijah foretold the death of his child and the ruin of his house.
Though blind with age, he knew the disguised queen at the door, for the LORD had shewed him heavy tidings.
scriptures: And he said to Jeroboam, Take thee ten pieces: for thus saith the LORD, the God of Israel, Behold, I will rend the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and will give ten tribes to thee.

And it came to pass at that time when Jeroboam went out of Jerusalem, that the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite found him in the way; and he had clad himself with a new garment; and they two were alone in the field.

And it was so, when Ahijah heard the sound of her feet, as she came in at the door, that he said, Come in, thou wife of Jeroboam; why feignest thou thyself to be another? for I am sent to thee with heavy tidings.
And they buried him; and all Israel mourned for him, according to the word of the LORD, which he spake by the hand of his servant Ahijah the prophet.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the temptation is to admire prophecy only when it flatters a cause and to forget that the same word judges the powers it once anointed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the impartiality of the prophetic word. Ahijah anointed Jeroboam for a purpose God ordained, the chastening of Solomon's house; the modern habit would then bind the prophet to the man's cause forever. But when Jeroboam corrupted the worship of God with his calves, the same prophet pronounced his ruin. The word of the LORD is no party banner; it raises kings and casts them down by one standard, the obedience of faith.

Ahijah's blindness and his certain knowledge of the disguised queen also rebuke the folly of thinking God can be deceived by appearances. Jeroboam dressed his wife as a stranger, supposing an old and sightless prophet would not know her; but the LORD sees not as man sees, and the prophet greeted her with her own name and heavy tidings at the door. No disguise hides the heart from the God who searches it, and no policy of statecraft outwits the word that has already written the end.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew 'Achiyyah, “the LORD is my brother,” with the gentilic ha-Shiloni, marking him a man of Shiloh, the old tabernacle town of Ephraim.
roots_lines: 'Ach, Hebrew, brother, joined to Yah, the covenant name, in his proper name.
Shiloh, the Ephraimite town where the tabernacle stood from Joshua until Eli's day.
The rent garment of twelve pieces is an enacted prophecy, common to the prophets, declaring by deed what the word announced.
Davar YHWH, “the word of the LORD,” the phrase that frames both his oracles, the raising and the ruin.
His “heavy tidings” (1 Kings 14:6) name the burden a faithful prophet must carry even to a king's house.
usage: He cited Ahijah to show that a true prophet condemns the very king he once anointed when that king forsakes God.
The teacher noted that the rent garment preached the division of the kingdom before a word of it came to pass.
“Why feignest thou thyself to be another?” the pastor read, and warned that no disguise hides the heart from God.

etymology: From the Latin legio, a Roman army division of some six thousand men, taken up into the Greek of the Gospels as the self-given name of the unclean spirits that possessed the Gadarene.
biblical_def: Legion is the name the unclean spirits gave themselves when our Lord demanded it of the demoniac among the tombs of the country of the Gadarenes (or Gergesenes). The man dwelt in the tombs, exceeding fierce, breaking chains and fetters, crying night and day and cutting himself with stones, an image of the ruin sin and Satan work upon the image-bearer. When Jesus came, the spirits cried out, owning Him as Son of the most high God, and besought Him not to torment them before the time. Asked his name, the man answered, “My name is Legion: for we are many”—a confession that a multitude of devils, numerous as a Roman legion, held one soul in bondage. The demons begged leave to enter the herd of swine, and our Lord granted it; the unclean spirits drove the unclean beasts, about two thousand, violently down the steep into the sea, where they were choked. The townsfolk, finding the man clothed and in his right mind, sitting at the feet of Jesus, were more afraid of the Deliverer than of the demoniac and begged Him to depart. Legion is the dictionary's standing proof of the reality, the malice, and the multitude of the powers of darkness, and of the absolute authority of Christ over them: a word from Him empties a soul that all the chains of men could not bind, for the strong man is bound by the Stronger.
webster_summary: The name given by the unclean spirits possessing the Gadarene demoniac, signifying their multitude; their expulsion into the swine displays the reality of the demonic and the absolute authority of Christ over the powers of darkness.
webster_full: LEGION, noun. [Latin, legio, a Roman military division of about six thousand.] A great multitude.
In the Gospels, the self-given name of the demons possessing the man among the tombs of the Gadarenes, “for we are many.”
The man was fierce and untameable, breaking every chain, until Christ commanded the spirits to come out.
The demons entered a herd of swine, which ran down a steep place into the sea and perished.
The delivered man was found clothed and in his right mind, sitting at the feet of Jesus.
scriptures: Mr 5:9
And he asked him, What is thy name? And he answered, saying, My name is Legion: for we are many.

And forthwith Jesus gave them leave. And the unclean spirits went out, and entered into the swine: and the herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea, (they were about two thousand;) and were choked in the sea.
And Jesus asked him, saying, What is thy name? And he said, Legion: because many devils were entered into him.

Then they went out to see what was done; and came to Jesus, and found the man, out of whom the devils were departed, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid.
corruption_summary: The modern temptation is to demythologize Legion into a case of mental illness, denying the personal reality of demons and the unique authority of Christ over them.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant academic reading reduces the demoniac to a sufferer of psychiatric disease and the swine to folklore, treating the demons as a primitive idiom for affliction. The dictionary rejects this on the authority of the text and of the Lord, who addressed the spirits as persons, received their answer, and granted their request to enter the swine. The drowning of two thousand beasts is not a symptom of one man's mind; it is an external, witnessed event that confirms the spirits were real, many, and now expelled. To demythologize Legion is to demythologize the Christ who cast them out.

Yet the dictionary distinguishes, as Scripture does, between demonic possession and the ordinary afflictions of body and soul. Not every torment is a devil, and the rise of an enthusiastic deliverance-ministry culture that finds a demon behind every sorrow is its own corruption, often kin to the hyper-charismatic excess the confession warns against. The sober ground is this: the powers of darkness are real and malicious, the Lord Jesus is sovereign over them, and the believer's safety is not in technique but in the authority of Christ, before whom a legion flees at a word.
roots_summary: From the Latin legio, the largest unit of the Roman army; the demons borrow the soldier's word to confess their multitude and their martial hostility against the soul of man.
roots_lines: Legio, Latin, a Roman legion of roughly six thousand foot with cavalry and auxiliaries.
Legeon, the Greek transliteration found in Mark and Luke.
The term confesses both number (“we are many”) and organized hostility, as of an army arrayed against a man.
Akathartos, Greek, unclean, the standing adjective for these spirits in the Gospels.
The swine, themselves unclean beasts under the law, fittingly receive the unclean spirits cast out.
usage: The pastor preached Legion to show that no chain of human strength can bind a soul that a word of Christ sets free.
He warned against both the modern denial of demons and the credulous habit of seeing one behind every trouble.
She saw in the man clothed and in his right mind the whole work of grace: the sinner seated at the feet of Jesus.

pos: noun phrase (a title of the Messiah)
etymology: From the Latin consolatio, comfort, rendering the Greek paraklesis; a title for the promised Messiah and the comfort He would bring, set in the mouth of aged Simeon.
biblical_def: The Consolation of Israel is the title under which devout Simeon waited for the Messiah, the long-promised Comforter of God's afflicted people. Luke records that there was in Jerusalem a man named Simeon, just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Ghost was upon him; it had been revealed to him that he should not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ. The phrase gathers up the whole prophetic hope of comfort that runs from Isaiah's “Comfort ye, comfort ye my people” through the latter chapters of that prophet, where the LORD promises to comfort Zion and to lay His salvation in Sion. When Simeon took the infant Jesus into his arms in the temple, he blessed God and sang that his eyes had seen the salvation prepared before the face of all people, a light to lighten the Gentiles and the glory of His people Israel. The consolation was therefore not a deliverance from Rome, as the carnal expectation supposed, but the advent of the Saviour Himself, whose person is the comfort of the afflicted and whose work brings the only lasting peace. The dictionary marks the title as a corrective to every merely political or therapeutic notion of comfort: the consolation of Israel is a Person, the incarnate Son, and the comfort of the gospel is the forgiveness of sins and reconciliation to God, not the easing of outward circumstance.
webster_summary: A title of the promised Messiah, the Comforter for whom devout Simeon waited; fulfilled when he took the infant Christ in his arms and blessed God for the salvation prepared before all people.
webster_full: CONSOLATION OF ISRAEL, noun phrase. [Latin consolatio, comfort.] A title of the Messiah as the promised Comforter of God's people.
Aged Simeon, just and devout, waited for the consolation of Israel, with the Holy Ghost upon him.
It was revealed to him that he should not die before seeing the Lord's Christ.
Taking the infant Jesus in the temple, he sang that his eyes had seen God's salvation.
The consolation is a Person—the incarnate Saviour, the light of the Gentiles and the glory of Israel.
scriptures: And, behold, there was a man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon; and the same man was just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel: and the Holy Ghost was upon him.
For mine eyes have seen thy salvation,
A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel.
Isa 40:1
Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God.
corruption_summary: The modern therapeutic age would reduce “consolation” to emotional comfort and self-soothing, severing it from the Christ who is Himself the comfort of His people.
corruption_paragraphs: Therapy-culture has annexed the word “comfort” and made it mean the relief of distress and the management of feeling. The biblical consolation of Israel is of a wholly different order: it is the coming of the Saviour to deal with sin, to reconcile rebels to God, and to give a peace the world cannot give or take away. Simeon did not wait for an easing of his circumstances; he waited for a Person, and held Him in his arms. The dictionary names the substitution of self-soothing for the Christ as the corruption of the age, and recovers comfort as a fruit of the gospel, not a technique of the self.

Equally, the carnal expectation of Simeon's day looked for a political consolation—deliverance from Rome and the restoration of an earthly kingdom. The Lord's salvation was deeper and wider: a light to lighten the Gentiles as well as the glory of Israel. The dictionary holds both errors at bay: the consolation of Israel is neither a political program nor a feeling, but the incarnate Son in whom God comforts His afflicted people by saving them from their sins.
roots_summary: From the Greek paraklesis (a calling alongside to comfort or exhort), rendered consolatio in the Latin; the same root names the Holy Ghost as the Comforter (Parakletos).
roots_lines: Paraklesis, Greek, comfort, encouragement, the noun behind Simeon's hope.
Parakletos, the cognate title of the Holy Spirit, the Comforter, in John's Gospel.
Consolatio, Latin, the Vulgate rendering, source of the English title.
The Isaianic “comfort ye my people” (Isaiah 40:1) is the prophetic root of the expectation.
Simeon's song, the Nunc Dimittis, frames the consolation as a Person beheld and embraced.
usage: At the funeral the pastor read Simeon's song, that the consolation of Israel is a Person who holds His people as Simeon held Him.
He distinguished the gospel's comfort from the world's self-soothing, naming the difference the difference of Christ.
She waited for the consolation of Israel as Simeon did, looking not for ease but for the Saviour Himself.

etymology: From the Latin virtus (strength, worth), rendering the Hebrew 'eshet chayil, “a woman of strength, worth, or valour”; the closing portrait of Proverbs.
biblical_def: The virtuous woman is the crowning portrait of the book of Proverbs, the acrostic poem of chapter thirty-one that sets forth the godly wife and mother as a woman of strength and worth whose price is far above rubies. The Hebrew 'eshet chayil describes not a passive ornament but a woman of valour: she works willingly with her hands, riseth while it is yet night to give meat to her household, considereth a field and buyeth it, planteth a vineyard, stretcheth out her hand to the poor and needy, maketh fine linen and selleth it, openeth her mouth with wisdom, and in her tongue is the law of kindness. The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her; her children arise up and call her blessed; her husband praiseth her in the gates. The poem refuses the world's twin lies about womanhood—that worth lies in favour and beauty, which are deceitful and vain, and that the home is a small and slighted sphere. Her industry, enterprise, and strength are poured out within and from the household she governs, and the secret of all of it is named in the final verse: a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised. The dictionary holds this chapter as the biblical standard of femininity over against both the older sentimentality that made the wife a frail decoration and the newer ideology that despises the home; she is strong, capable, and praised, and she is so as a wife and mother who fears God in the complementary order of creation.
webster_summary: The Hebrew 'eshet chayil, the “woman of valour” of Proverbs 31, whose strength, industry, and wisdom are poured out in the fear of the LORD; the biblical standard of godly womanhood.
webster_full: VIRTUOUS WOMAN, noun phrase. [Hebrew 'eshet chayil, a woman of strength or worth.] The godly wife and mother portrayed in Proverbs 31.
Her price is far above rubies; the heart of her husband safely trusteth in her.
She works willingly with her hands, governs her household, deals in field and merchandise, and stretches out her hand to the poor.
She openeth her mouth with wisdom, and the law of kindness is in her tongue.
Favour is deceitful and beauty vain, but a woman that feareth the LORD shall be praised.
scriptures: Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies.
The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her, so that he shall have no need of spoil.
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.
And now, my daughter, fear not; I will do to thee all that thou requirest: for all the city of my people doth know that thou art a virtuous woman.
corruption_summary: The portrait is corrupted both by an older sentimentality that made the wife a frail ornament and by a newer ideology that despises the home and recasts her industry as proof against the complementary order.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern egalitarian readings seize on the virtuous woman's commerce and enterprise to argue that Proverbs 31 overturns the complementary order of Scripture, as though her field-buying and merchandising proved the home an unworthy sphere. The dictionary names this as a corruption of the passage. The woman of valour is praised precisely as a wife whose husband's heart trusts in her and as a mother whose children call her blessed; her strength is poured out within and from a household she governs under her husband's headship. Her capability is no argument against the created order but the flowering of a woman who fears the LORD inside it.

The opposite corruption is the older sentimentality that made the godly wife a frail and idle decoration, valued for favour and beauty—the very things the poem calls deceitful and vain. Scripture's woman is strong, industrious, wise, and generous, rising before dawn and opening her mouth with wisdom. The dictionary recovers the whole portrait: neither a feminist proof-text nor a Victorian ornament, but a woman of valour whose worth is her fear of God and whose sphere is the household and all that flows from it.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew 'eshet chayil, a woman of chayil (strength, force, worth, valour), the same word used of mighty men of war; the Latin virtus behind “virtuous” carries the same note of strength.
roots_lines: 'Ishshah, Hebrew, woman or wife, the subject of the acrostic poem.
Chayil, Hebrew, strength, force, worth, ability—used elsewhere of armies and valiant men.
Virtus, Latin, strength and worth, the root of the English “virtuous,” which once meant powerful, not merely well-behaved.
The acrostic form (each verse beginning with a successive Hebrew letter) frames her praise as an ordered whole.
The same word chayil is spoken over Ruth (Ruth 3:11), binding the Moabitess to the ideal of Proverbs 31.
usage: He preached Proverbs 31 to honour the labouring mothers of the congregation as women of valour, not idle ornaments.
She taught her daughters that favour and beauty fade, but the fear of the LORD makes a woman praised.
The elder rebuked the notion that the home is a small sphere, pointing to all the virtuous woman governs from it.

pos: noun phrase (the ark of the flood)
etymology: From the Hebrew tevah, a chest or vessel (the same word used of the basket of the infant Moses); the great vessel of gopher wood in which Noah and his house were saved through the flood.
biblical_def: Noah's ark was the great vessel of gopher wood, three hundred cubits long, which the LORD commanded Noah to build for the saving of his house when He purposed to destroy the earth with a flood of waters for its violence and corruption. It was pitched within and without with pitch, divided into rooms and three stories, lighted by a window and entered by a single door. Into it went Noah and his wife, his three sons and their wives—eight souls—and of every living thing two of every sort, and of the clean beasts by sevens, that seed might be kept alive upon the face of the earth. When all were in, the text says with solemn weight that the LORD shut him in; the door of salvation was closed by God's own hand. The waters prevailed and every living thing in whose nostrils was the breath of life died, save those the ark bore safely upon the deep. The ark is no fable: it stands in Scripture as a true history of judgment and mercy and as a great type of salvation. Peter declares that the eight souls were saved by water, the like figure whereunto baptism doth also now save us; the single door prefigures the one way of salvation in Christ; and the shut door warns that the day of grace has a term. The dictionary holds the historicity of Noah, the ark, and the worldwide flood, and reads the vessel as the figure of Christ, in whom alone the household of faith rides out the deluge of God's righteous wrath.
webster_summary: The great vessel of gopher wood in which Noah, his household of eight, and the creatures were preserved through the worldwide flood; a true history and a type of salvation in Christ, into which the LORD Himself shut the saved.
webster_full: NOAH'S ARK, noun phrase. [Hebrew tevah, a chest or vessel.] The ship of gopher wood, three hundred cubits long, built by Noah at God's command.
It preserved Noah, his wife, his three sons and their wives—eight souls—and pairs of every living kind through the flood.
It was pitched within and without, with rooms, three stories, a window, and a single door.
When all were within, the LORD shut him in, and the waters prevailed over the earth.
A type of salvation: the eight saved by water prefigure baptism (1 Peter 3:20-21), and the one door, the one Saviour.
scriptures: Make thee an ark of gopher wood; rooms shalt thou make in the ark, and shalt pitch it within and without with pitch.
Ge 7:1
And the LORD said unto Noah, Come thou and all thy house into the ark; for thee have I seen righteous before me in this generation.
And they that went in, went in male and female of all flesh, as God had commanded him: and the LORD shut him in.
Which sometime were disobedient, when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was a preparing, wherein few, that is, eight souls were saved by water.
corruption_summary: Modern criticism recasts the ark and the flood as borrowed myth or local legend, denying their history and emptying the type of its force.
corruption_paragraphs: The historical-critical mainstream treats Noah's ark as a religious adaptation of older flood myths and the deluge as, at most, a local Mesopotamian inundation dressed in theological language. The dictionary rejects this framing. Our Lord Himself spoke of the days of Noe as real history and the very pattern of His coming (Matthew 24:37-39); Peter and the writer to the Hebrews treat Noah, the ark, and the flood as fact. To make the account a baptized myth is to unsettle the words of Christ and the apostles, who built doctrine upon its truth.

The recovery is to read the ark as both history and type. It is a real vessel that bore eight real souls through a real judgment; and it is a figure of salvation in Christ. The single door declares the one way of escape (John 14:6); the pitch (Hebrew kopher, akin to the word for atonement) hints at the covering that keeps out the waters of wrath; and the LORD who shut Noah in teaches that salvation is God's closing act, not man's. The shut door also sounds a warning: the longsuffering of God has a term, and the day comes when the door is shut.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew tevah, a chest or ark, used only of this vessel and of the basket of Moses; both bear the saved through deadly waters, binding the two deliverances together.
roots_lines: Tevah, Hebrew, a chest or box-like vessel, used of Noah's ark and of the ark of bulrushes that bore Moses.
Gopher, the unidentified wood (perhaps cypress) of which the ark was made.
Kopher, the pitch with which it was sealed, from a root meaning to cover, kin to kippur, atonement.
The dimensions in cubits mark a vessel of vast and stable proportion, not a mythic conceit.
The “door” (Hebrew pethach) shut by the LORD frames salvation as God's sovereign act.
usage: The pastor preached that the LORD shut Noah in, that salvation might be seen as God's act and not man's grip.
He pointed to the single door of the ark as a figure of the one Saviour through whom the household of faith is saved.
She taught the children the flood as true history, for the Lord Jesus spoke of the days of Noah as a pattern of His coming.
